Until v1.1, defMIKUMARI.vhd is described with VHDL-2008.

From v2.0, no source file written with VHDL-2008.

docs.title: CDCM based transceiver (CBT)
docs.text:
The CBT is a physical layer of the MIKUMARI system. About the CBT, see also Ref. The roles of the CBT are as follows.

  • Encode and decode the CDCM modulated waveform pattern
  • Defines three types of CBT character using sign extension from 8-bit to 10-bit
  • Initialize IOSERDES when detecting the cable (fiber) connection

Currently, the CBT supports the CDCM-10-2.5, CDCM-10-1.5, CDCM-8-2.5, and CDCM-8-1.5. Then, the frequency ratios between the serial and parallel clock signals are 5 for CDCM-10-XX and 4 for CDCM-8-XX with the double-data-rate (DDR) mode, respectively. The SDR mode is not supported. In addition, only the differential signal is supported. If you want to use the Local Area Common Clock Protocol (LACCP), you need to select CDCM-8-XX modes. The serdesOffset port does not work with CDCM-10-XX modes.

docs.title: Interface of CBT
docs.text: CbtLane is the top-level CBT module. Types and width constants are defined in defCDCM.vhd.

docs.title: Generics
docs.text:
Generics without a default must be specified when instantiating CbtLane.

Generic Description kFamily FPGA family: "7S" for 7-series; "US" for UltraScale/UltraScale+. kCdcmModWidth CDCM time slices: 8 for CDCM-8; 10 for CDCM-10. kIoStandardTx TX differential output buffer I/O standard. kTxPolarity Invert TX polarity when true. genIDELAYCTRL Instantiate IDELAYCTRL when true. kDiffTerm Enable differential input termination when true. kRxPolarity Invert RX polarity when true. kIoStandardRx RX differential input buffer I/O standard. kIoDelayGroup IODELAY_GROUP for IDELAYCTRL and delay primitives. kFixIdelayTap Use tapValueIn for initialization instead of automatic tap adjustment when true. kFreqFastClk SERDES serial clock frequency in MHz. kFreqRefClk IDELAYCTRL reference clock frequency in MHz. kBitslice0 Set true when RX uses BITSLICE_0 on UltraScale devices. kNumEncodeBits CDCM payload bits per clkPar cycle: 1 for 1.5 modes; 2 for 2.5 modes. kCbtMode CBT operating mode: "Master" or "Slave". enDebug Enable the preset mark_debug attributes.

docs.title: Clock/Reset
docs.text: Port Direction Description srst In Active-high reset for clkPar logic and the transceiver. pwrOnRst In Active-high reset for logic driven by clkIndep and clkIdelayRef. clkSerTx In Serial TX clock from BUFG: 5 x clkPar for CDCM-10; 4 x clkPar for CDCM-8. clkSerRx In Serial RX clock from BUFG: 5 x clkPar for CDCM-10; 4 x clkPar for CDCM-8. clkPar In Parallel clock from BUFG. clkIndep In Independent clock for the clock monitor. clkIdelayRef In IDELAYCTRL reference clock, independent of clkPar.

docs.title: Initialization/Status
docs.text: Port Direction Description initIn In Restart initialization. Synchronous to clkPar. tapValueIn In IDELAY tap setting used when kFixIdelayTap is true. reqIdelayShift In "00": no adjustment; "01": increase delay by one step of tapValueOut; "10": decrease by one step; "11": reserved. reqShutOffOut Out Request the upper-layer protocol to suspend communication for readjustment. shutOffAckIn In Upper-layer acknowledgement of reqShutOffOut. delayPerTap Out Delay per tap in picoseconds. cbtLaneUp Out High when the CBT is ready for communication. tapValueOut Out Current IDELAY tap setting. bitslipNum Out Current bitslip position; also updated during CDCM-8 dynamic adjustment. serdesOffset Out Signed phase offset between the input bit pattern and clkPar for LACCP (CDCM-8 only). firstBitPatt Out ISERDES pattern captured after IDELAY adjustment, before bitslip. cntValueOutInit Out Initial master delay counter value (CNTVALUEOUT) for UltraScale CDCM-8; zero on 7-series. cntValueOutSlaveInit Out Initial slave delay counter value (CNTVALUEOUT) for UltraScale CDCM-8; zero on 7-series. patternErr Out A received waveform violates the CDCM pattern. idelayErr Out IDELAY adjustment failed. bitslipErr Out SERDES bitslip failed to find the expected pattern. watchDogErr Out Watchdog timeout; the other endpoint appears to be down.

docs.title: Data I/F
docs.text: Port Direction Description isKTypeTx In TX character type: 1 for K-type; 0 for D-type. dataInTx In 8-bit TX user data. validInTx In High when dataInTx is valid; low requests an idle pattern. txBeat Out Indicates the encoder character cycle. txAck Out Acknowledges acceptance of valid TX data. isIdleRx Out High when the received character is idle. isKTypeRx Out RX character type: 1 for K-type; 0 for D-type. dataOutRx Out 8-bit RX user data. validOutRx Out High when dataOutRx is valid.

docs.title: Physical I/F
docs.text: Port Direction Description cdcmTxp Out Positive differential TX output. Connect to the top-level port. cdcmTxn Out Negative differential TX output. Connect to the top-level port. cdcmRxp In Positive differential RX input. Connect to the top-level port. cdcmRxn In Negative differential RX input. Connect to the top-level port. modClock Out Received modulated clock. For UltraScale CDCM-8 with kBitslice0=true, outputs a virtual clock.

docs.title: CBT characters
docs.text: The CBT character is a 10-bit internal data format in the CBT and is generated by simply adding 2-bit type header to a 8-bit data. There are K-, D-, and T-types characters. In addition, there is a IDLE character, which consists of the modulated signal with the duty ration of 50%. The T-type characters are used to control the CBT, and they are hidden inside the CBT. K-type characters are used to control the link protocol, and their bit pattern are defined in the CBT level. D-type characters are user data. The transmission request for D- and K-type characters are exclusive because it is determined by isKTypeTx signal. However, T-type character transmission can conflict with D- and K-type characters. The transmission priority among characters is defined as D < T < K characters. During the T-type character transmission, D-type character transmission is held up. The link protocol needs to keep the current dataInTx until the txAck is returned.

docs.title: CDCM encode and decode
docs.text: Currently, the CBT supports CDCM-10-1.5 (CDCM-8-1.5) and CDCM-10-2.5; they can transmit 1-bit binary + idle pattern and 2-bit binary + idle pattern per clkPar cycle, respectively. For details, see Ref and Ref. Since the CBT character has 10-bit data width, 10 and 5 clock cycles are necessary to send a CBT character by CDCM-10-1.5 (CDCM-8-1.5) and CDCM-10-2.5, respectively. CDCM-10-1.5 (CDCM-8-1.5) has longer latency while it provides the better jitter performance because the duty cycle change range is narrower than that of CDCM-10-2.5.

docs.title: Initialization process
docs.text: CbtLane initializes the receive sampling delay, the SERDES bit position, and the CBT character boundary before completing the Master/Slave handshake. The sequence depends on kCbtMode.

docs.title: Reset and restart conditions
docs.text:
srst resets the transceiver and the clkPar logic. pwrOnRst resets the independent-domain logic and IDELAY initialization logic. Initialization proceeds after reset and internal initialization requests are released; deasserting initIn alone does not immediately start the sequence because its request is stretched internally for more than 2 * kMaxWDT cycles of clkPar.

Mode Initialization requests generated by CbtLane "Master" The stretched initIn request, RX clock loss detected by ClockMonitor, or an internal reset interval triggered by the RX quality monitor or watchDogErr. ClockMonitor uses clkIndep; clock loss holds the receiver in initialization until the RX clock is detected again. "Slave" The stretched initIn request or the RX quality monitor request. No ClockMonitor is instantiated in this mode.

In both modes, CbtRx also requests reinitialization on a watchdog timeout or a handshake timeout. On 7-series devices with genIDELAYCTRL=true, SERDES initialization waits for IDELAYCTRL RDY. For UltraScale CDCM-8 automatic adjustment, it waits for the initial master and slave IDELAY counter values to be captured.

docs.title: Sampling delay and SERDES alignment
docs.text:
With kFixIdelayTap=false, the receiver scans the IDELAY settings, checks for an unchanged sampled idle pattern, and selects the center of a sufficiently wide stable region. With kFixIdelayTap=true, it loads tapValueIn and still checks sample stability before proceeding. The selected setting is reported by tapValueOut.

After IDELAY adjustment, the receiver captures firstBitPatt and performs bitslip until the sampled pattern matches kIdleCDCM for 16 consecutive checks (kPattOkThreshold). In the RTL's bit-vector order, kIdleCDCM is 00000_11111 for CDCM-10. CDCM-8 uses 0000_1111, padded with a leading 0 and a trailing 1 for the same internal 10-bit comparison. Completion of IDELAY adjustment and bitslip sets the internal status to kInitFinish; this does not yet assert cbtLaneUp.

docs.title: Master/Slave handshake
docs.text:
The receiver state machine controls its local transmitter through the internal back channel. SendZero disables transmission by sending an all-zero pattern, SendIdle sends the idle pattern, and SendInitPattern alternates kInitPCDCM and kInitMCDCM. The initialization T-type characters I1 and I2 are selected by GetInit1Char(kNumEncodeBits) and GetInit2Char(kNumEncodeBits).

Stage Master Slave Local SERDES initialization Sends idle until its local status reaches kInitFinish, then sends the initialization waveform. Sends zero until its local status reaches kInitFinish, then sends idle. Initialization waveform detection Counts 16 received kInitPCDCM or kInitMCDCM patterns after kInitFinish, then sends I1. Counts the same 16 patterns, then sends the initialization waveform. CBT character alignment Sends I1 and enables decoder alignment. Once aligned, sends I2. Sends the initialization waveform and enables decoder alignment. Once aligned, sends I1. Readiness confirmation Counts eight valid received I2 characters, then enters StateCbtRxUp. On the first valid received I2, starts sending I2. It then counts eight valid received characters other than I2 before entering StateCbtRxUp.

CdcmRxDecoder aligns the CBT character boundary to I1 separately from the SERDES bitslip. The initialization waveform and readiness counters accumulate matches; they do not require consecutive matches. Initialization T-type characters are handled internally, and user TX data is not acknowledged during these handshake stages.

CbtRx asserts its internal RX-up status in StateCbtRxUp; CbtTx asserts TX-up on an encoder beat in that state. cbtLaneUp is asserted when both are high and their conjunction has propagated through the 128-stage clkPar delay pipeline (kDelayLaneUp).

If IDELAY adjustment or bitslip fails, idelayErr or bitslipErr is asserted and the corresponding adjustment state machine retries. A handshake timeout causes CbtRx to restart initialization.

docs.title: Error detection
docs.text:
When cbtLaneUp is high, the CBT checks whether the sampled bit pattern is matched with the CDCM encoding rule or not. If a broken pattern is detected, the patternErr signal is asserted, but at this moment, the CBT is not reset. If more than 1% of received bit pattern are broken, the RX quality check monitor requests to reset the CBT.

When cbtLaneUp is high, the CBT transmits the T-type character, dogfood character, periodically. The dogfood character resets the watch dog timer in other side. If the watch dog timer can't eat dogfood within specified time, the watchDogErr goes high, and the watchdog timer requests to reset the CBT.

docs.title: MIKUMARI
docs.text:
The MIKUMARI link is a clock signal, timing, and synchronous command distribution protocol for front-end electronics (FEE) based on the clock-duty-cycle-modulation (CDCM). By distributing a modulated clock signal based on pulse width modulation (PWM), it is possible to transmit both clock signal and data on a single transmission line while achieving clock recovery without a dedicated clock-data-recovery (CDR) circuit. The MIKUMARI link consists of the CDCM based transceiver (CBT) and the link layer protocol, the MIKUMARI link. The CBT provides the functionalities of the physical layer, and the MIKUMARI link defines the communication protocol between physically connected link end points.

The MIKUMARI link is vender IP independent except for the serializer/de-serializer block in the CBT. Currently, the CBT is implemented for AMD Xilinx FPGAs using the IOSERDES primitive.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The minimum configuration of the MIKUMARI link is shown in the figure. The left and right hand sides are the primary and the secondary nodes, respectively. The purpose of the MIKUMARI link is distributing the reference clock signal to all the FEEs, and then a root module may have an oscillator. To operate the system, two skew adjusted clock signals are necessary. One is the parallel clock signal to drive the parallel data path, and the other is the serial clock signal to drive the transmission line. In many cases, the reference clock will be equal to the parallel clock. The frequency ratio between the serial and parallel clock signals is defined by the modulation pattern. If the CDCM-10-XX (See Ref.) is used, the developer has to prepare the 5 times faster serial clock signal than that of the parallel clock, and 4 times faster clock signal is necessary for CDCM-8-XX. The maximum transferable reference (parallel) clock frequency is determined by the maximum acceptable clock signal frequency of the clock buffer in FPGA or the maximum data rate of IO pads. For example for Kintex-7 with the speed-grate -1 and the FBG package, the maximum BUFG speed and the maximum IO rate are 625 MHz and 1250 Mbps (HP bank case), and then the maximum transferable parallel clock speed is 125 MHz with CDCM-10-XX.

In the secondary side, these clock signals are reproduced from the modulated clock signal by a PLL on FEEs. Many PLL devices, i.e., PLLs in FPGA, external PLL ICs, and external jitter cleaner ICs, will work as a clock recovery circuit. To obtain the good jitter performance, the PLL of which the phase noise is low should be selected. The jitter distribution depends on the selected PLL device. As discussed in Ref, the obtained jitter rms when using MMCM in Kintex-7 FPGA is worse than that of the external jitter cleaner IC, CDCE62002. This comes not from the main peak structure but from the tail structure mainly. In author's opinion, MMCM is enough for 1 ns TDC synchronization, but it is not enough for high-resolution TDC with the precision around 30 ps. From the view point of the clock phase uncertainty, the PLL should have a zero-delay mode. As the CDCM technique recovers the parallel clock from the modulated clock, the phase uncertainty of the recovered clock does not appear if the PLL has the zero-delay mode. This is the important difference between the CDR circuit, which reproduced the serial clock. Unavoidable phase uncertainty exists due to the frequency division.

Figure 1: The minimum configuration of the MIKUMARI system.

Since the MIKUMARI system aims to distribute the reference clock signal to synchronize FEEs, the connection topology of the MIKUMARI link should be a tree structure starting from a root module. If the root module cannot drive all FEEs, a fan-out module is necessary in intermediate layers. An example of fan-out is shown in the figure. As the CBT and the MIKUMARI link are defined as the full-duplex transceiver and the link protocol for point-to-point communication, respectively, a simple signal fan-out is not allowed. In fan-out module, the clock signals are once recovered and drive the CBTs transferring the modulated clock signal to downstream modules. In many applications, all FEEs will receive the same command from the primary module, and then TX data can be broadcasted, however, a user circuit summarizing information from the downstream modules may be necessary in the RX side. However, this is not mandatory. Since the TX and RX of the MIKUMARI link are independent, the RX port of the right side can be left open if you decide not to use the uplink data path. Since the validOutRx and frameLastOutRx signals are one-shot, the RX port and the TX ports cannot be directly connected due to the txAck cycle. Therefore, the TxElasticBuffer is necessary to connect the RX and TX ports. The TxElasticBuffer is a simple queuing buffer for adjusting CBT character transfer cycle.

Figure 2: Example of fan-out.

The MIKUMARI link does not have a routing function, and then it does not support the end-to-end (source to destination) communication. Therefore, the clock signal, timing, and synchronous data transmissions are realized by repeating the point-to-point communication in the link layer. Thus, arbitrariness exists in the connection scheme inside the fan-out module. The MIKUMARI link protocol does not include experimental specific functions. It just provides the functionalities for sending a one-shot pulse with the fixed latency and the normal data transmission using the frame structure. An upper layer protocol, which provides dedicated functions for each experiment, is additionally necessary when using this system in actual experiments.

docs.title: MIKUMARI link protocol
docs.text:
The MIKUMARI link is a link layer protocol to establish the communication link between two end points, which are physically connected. The roles of the MIKUMARI link are as follows.

  • Define the K-type characters; these are characters for the link control.
  • Define a frame structure, called the MIKUMARI frame, for the data transmission
  • One-shot pulse transmission with fixed latency using K-type characters.

docs.title: Interface of MIKUMARI link
docs.text: MikumariLane is the top-level MIKUMARI link module. Protocol constants and pulse types are defined in defMikumari.vhd; CBT data types are defined in defCDCM.vhd.

docs.title: Generics
docs.text: Generic Description kNumEncodeBits CDCM payload bits per clkPar cycle: 1 for 1.5 modes; 2 for 2.5 modes. Match the CBT setting. enScrambler Enable the data scrambler and descrambler when true. kHighPrecision Select High-Precision pulse mode when true; Low-Latency mode when false. enDEBUG Enable the preset mark_debug attributes.

docs.title: System port
docs.text: Port Direction Description srst In Active-high reset for the MIKUMARI link. clkPar In Parallel clock from BUFG. Use the same clock as the CBT. cbtUpIn In CBT ready signal. Connect to CbtLane.cbtLaneUp. linkUp Out High when the MIKUMARI link is established.

docs.title: TX port
docs.text: Port Direction Description dataInTx In 8-bit TX frame payload. validInTx In High when dataInTx is valid. frameLastInTx In High when dataInTx is the last byte of the frame payload. txAck Out Acknowledges acceptance of valid TX data. pulseIn In One-cycle pulse transmission request. Accepted when busyPulseTx is low. pulseTypeTx In 3-bit pulse type, latched when pulseIn is accepted. pulseRegTx In 4-bit extra pulse data, latched when pulseIn is accepted in High-Precision mode. busyPulseTx Out High while a pulse is reserved or being transmitted; pulseIn is ignored. isKtypeOut Out High when cbtDataOut is K-type. Connect to CbtLane.isKTypeTx. cbtDataOut Out 8-bit data for the CBT. Connect to CbtLane.dataInTx. cbtValidOut Out High when cbtDataOut is valid. Connect to CbtLane.validInTx. cbtTxAck In CBT TX acknowledgement. Connect to CbtLane.txAck. cbtTxBeat In CBT character transmission cycle indicator. Connect to CbtLane.txBeat.

docs.title: RX port
docs.text: Port Direction Description dataOutRx Out 8-bit RX frame payload. validOutRx Out High when dataOutRx is valid. frameLastRx Out High when dataOutRx is the last byte of the frame payload. checksumErr Out Checksum mismatch in the received frame. frameBroken Out Frame payload received without a frame start K-type character (FSK). recvTermnd Out FSK received before the previous frame's frame end K-type character (FEK). pulseOut Out Reproduced one-shot pulse. pulseTypeRx Out Received 3-bit pulse type, valid when pulseOut is high. pulseRegRx Out Received 4-bit extra pulse data, valid with pulseOut in High-Precision mode; zero in Low-Latency mode. isKtypeIn In High when cbtDataIn is K-type. Connect to CbtLane.isKTypeRx. cbtDataIn In 8-bit data from the CBT. Connect to CbtLane.dataOutRx. cbtValidIn In High when cbtDataIn is valid. Connect to CbtLane.validOutRx.

docs.title: MIKUMARI frame and data transmission
docs.text:
The MIKUMARI protocol transmits the data using a simple frame structure, called the MIKUMARI frame. The frame consists of four blocks as follows.

  • Frame start K-type character (FSK)
  • Arbitral length data body (payload)
  • 8-bit checksum
  • Frame end K-type character (FEK)

The frame structure is similar that of Xilinx Aurora 8b/1b protocol. Inserting FSK, FEK, and checksum are done by the MIKUMARI link, and later two are inserted after detecting frameLastInTx. At the receiver side, frameLastOutRx assertion and checksum calculation are performed after detecting the FEK. Note that 8-bit checksum data does not appear from dataOutRx. It is internally used. About details of the frame structure, see also Ref.

Since the frame body and 8-bit checksum data are D-type character, their transmission request can be blocked by the T-type character transmission by the CBT. If it is blocked, the txAck is not returned at the expected timing, the upper layer protocol needs to keep the current dataInTx and validInTx until txAck is returned. It is defined that pulse K-type characters have higher priority to other K-type character in this protocol. Thus, FSK and FEK insertion can be delayed by pulse transmission request. Therefore, the data transmission latency using the MIKUMARI frame is not perfectly fixed. Use the pulse transfer function for usages where arrival times must be strictly controlled.

The data interface of the MIKUMARI link is also similar to that of Xilinx Aurora 8b/1b protocol (AXI4-stream). As there is the CBT character transmission cycle, txAck signal is used instead of tready signal.

The time chart for MIKUMARI data transmission is shown in the figure. The upper layer protocol sets the next data after detecting txAck high. If the data is last 1-byte of the frame body, assert frameLastInTx and keep it high until the next txAck high. The data 'D' is the 1st 1-byte of the data body in the next frame. We can suspend the data transmission by de-asserting validInTx. If validInTx is low at the txBeat timing, idle character is sent.

Figure 1: Time chart for MIKUMARI data transmission.

The time char for MIKUMARI data receive is shown in the figure. The validOutRx goes high when the dataOutRx is valid. If the dataOutRx is the last 1-byte of the frame, frameLastOutRx goes high at the same timing of validOutRx. After that, as checksum and K-type character receive continues, user data in the next frame will not appear immediately. Sometimes, validOutRx will not go high at the expected timing due to idle character receive or conflicting with K- or T-type characters.

Figure 2: Time chart for MIKUMARI data receive

docs.title: Pulse transmission
docs.text:
From version 2.0, the MIKUMARI-link protocol supports the high-precision mode for the pulse transmission. The original mode is called the low-latency mode to distingush them.

Low-latency mode

The pulse transmission with pulse types is realized by using K-type characters. The pulse type and the transmission request timing are encoded to a K-type character, and it is transmitted with highest priority. The receiver side decodes the received pulse K-type character and reproduces the pulse timing and the pulse type value. While the CBT character transmission is accepted once per 5 or 10 clock cycles, the pulse transmission can be requested at any timing. Due to the internal process realizing this feature, an additional idle character transmission is necessary after the pulse K-type character transmission. Therefore, the busy length for a pulse transfer is 10 and 20 clock cycles for CDCM-10-2.5 (CDCM-8-2.5) and CDCM-10-1.5 (CDCM-8-1.5), respectively. This limits the maximum pulse frequency. In addition, transmission of several pulse types at the same timing is also impossible.

Due to the limitation of the range of expressible bit combinations using 8-bit, the pulse K-type characters do not guarantee the DC balance of the signal on the transmission line. If the averaged duty ratio of the CDCM modulated clock is not 50%, the recovered clock signal phase is systematically shifted depending on the averaged duty ratio. This effect is visible when the pulse transfer rate is high. See Ref for the details.

High-precision mode

The 3-bit pulse type and the 4-bit extra data are encoded to two K-type characters. Thus, the pulse trasmission takes longer pulse transmission latency and the busy time than thoese of the low-latency mode. For the same reason, the miximu pulse transmission rate is also decreased. Instead, the high-precision mode ensures the DC balance perfectly. The phase shift of the recovered clock signal seen in the low-latency mode will not happen. This mode provides the better clock signal synchronization.

The author expects to use the extra 4-bit data to send information for the finer timing comepensation. For example, you can implement the 1-ns 3-bit TDC measuring the input pulse timing in the primary side (clkPar frequency is expected to be 125 MHz), and the TDC value is sent to the secondary side. Thus, you achieve the 1-ns timing trasmission.

docs.title: Data scrambler
docs.text: The MIKUMARI link supports the data scrambling based on PRBS16. Since the data scrambler guarantees the DC balance on average and there is no demerit, the author strongly recommend to use it.

docs.title: Checksum error
docs.text:
The checksumErr goes high, if the received checksum value and the calculated value is not the same. The MIKUMARI link do nothing even if the checksum error is detected. When the error is detected, error handring is left to the upper layer protocol. This signal indicates that the communication error for D-type characters happens. If the checksum error happens, the checksumErr signal goes high at the same timing of the frameLastRX signal as shown in the figure.

Figure 3: Timing chart for checksum error

docs.title: Frame broken
docs.text:
The data frame of the MIKUMARI-link protocol is defined as the D-type characters sandwitched by FSK and FEK. The frame broken signal goes high, if the D-type characters are received without detecting FSK. Since the frame starting position is unknown, all the data in this frame are invalid. The frame broken signal goes high instead of the validOutRx signal as shown in the figure.

Figure 4: Timing chart for frame broken

docs.title: Receive terminated
docs.text:
The recvTernd signal represents taht the frame receive process is terminated. This signal goes high if the FSK is received without detecting the FEK for the previous frame as shown in the figure. Since the frame end position of the 1st frame in the figure, the frame receive is terminated and it restarts immediately. Then, the 2nd frame in the figure is valid.

Figure 5: Timing chart for receive terminated

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Corrected pulse busy handling in MikumariTx.
    • busyPulseTx remains high while a pulse is reserved or being transmitted.
    • Requests on pulseIn are ignored while busy in both Low-Latency and High-Precision modes.

docs.title: Improved
docs.text: • Aligned HDL comments with the implementation, including serial clock ratios, IDELAY adjustment steps, error signals, and pulse mode behavior.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• Dynamic delay adjustment during communication
    • The Master CBT can readjust IDELAY after link-up in response to external reqIdelayShift requests.
    • For CDCM-8, adjustment at the tap-range boundary also shifts the bit-buffer window. The reqShutOffOut and shutOffAckIn ports coordinate temporary suspension and restart of communication with the upper-layer protocol.
    • The new delayPerTap output reports the IDELAY delay per tap in picoseconds.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Corrected the plateau search and threshold comparison in the 7-series automatic IDELAY adjustment algorithm.
    • Regions narrower than the required threshold are rejected. Regions whose length equals the threshold are now accepted.

docs.title: New + Improved
docs.text:
• Improved the automatic IDELAY adjustment algorithm.
    • The tap value is set to the midpoint of a stable region using its detected left and right edges.
  • Added a bit buffer for 7-series CDCM-8 receivers.
    • The IserdesBitslip module replaces the ISERDESE2 primitive's BITSLIP function with bit-window selection in logic.

docs.title: New
docs.text: • Applicable devices have been expanded to AMD Xilinx UltraScale/UltraScale+ FPGAs.

docs.title: Improved
docs.text:
• Enable again the clock monitor function
    • It was found that the clock monitor function is essential to deterministically set the IDELAY tap value in the initialization process.
  • Slightly modify the CDCM-RX initialization process.

docs.title: New + Improved
docs.text:
• High-precision mode of MIKUMARI pulse
    • The MIKUMARI pulse function newly supports the high-precision mode. This mode can transmit the 4-bit extra data together with the pulse, i.e., the 3-bit pulse type and the 4-bit data are simultaneously transferred. The existing pulse transmission mode is called the low-latency mode.
  • CBT serdesOffset and firstBitPatt ports
    • The serdesOffset and firstBitPatt ports are added to the CbtLane. The serdesOffset port provides the relative phase between the input bit pattern and the ClkPar signal. This port is for the Local Area Common Clock Protocol (LACCP).
    • The firstBitPatt port provides the bit pattern before starting the bit-slip process. This port is for debug.
  • Support CDCM-8-2.5
    • CDCM-8-2.5 was tested with Kintex-7 FPGA with thr reference clock signal frequency of 125 MHz. MMCM was used for the clock signal recovery.
  • Disable the clock monitor function
    • The clock monitor function in the CBT was disabled.

docs.title: New + Improved
docs.text:
• Add pwrOnRst port to CbtLane
    • CbtLane has single reset input so far despite using several clock signals. Logics driven by clkPar and logics driven by clkIndep and clkIdelayRef should not be reset by the same reset signal. To fix this, another reset signal, pwrOnRst, is introduced; it is expected that this reset is generated by the PLL lock signal, which generates clkIndep and clkIdelayRef signals.

docs.title: MikumariBlock
docs.text: The MikumariBlock is a wrapper module including the CbtLane and the MikumariLane. The intermediate signals between the CBT and the MIKUMARI link are hidden. For users, the author recommends to use the MikumariBlock. The almost all MikumariBlock entity ports are directly connected to the CBT and the MikumariLane entity ports. The reset asynchronous is available, finally input to the MikumariBlock is .

docs.title: Clock Configuration
docs.text: This section provides an example of using the MIKUMARI modulated clock with a frequency of 125 MHz and the CDCM-8-XX modulation pattern.

docs.title: 7-series FPGAs
docs.text:
The figure shows an example of a clock configuration for a 7-series 7 FPGA. This example uses an MMCM for clock recovery, but the MMCM can also be replaced with an external PLL. The example shown assumes that the reference clock frequency transmitted via the MIKUMARI link is 125 MHz. clkidctrl must be set to 200 MHz. Do not select a clkIndep frequency that is an integer multiple (including 1) of clkPar. In the 7-series, clkSerTx and Rx can be clocked from the same source.

The MMCM includes a function to align the phases of the input and output clocks. As a result, clkPar can be obtained with a deterministic phase relationship relative to the modulated clock input (modClk). Because of this characteristic, MMCMs generated from the IP catalog can be applied directly to 7-series FPGAs.

Figure 1: Clock configuration for the 7-series FPGAs.

docs.title: UlstraScale FPGAs
docs.text:
With UltraScale FPGAs, using an MMCM generated from the IP catalog as-is does not minimize skew between multiple clock signals; therefore, a more complex clock configuration than that used with 7-series FPGAs is required. For details, refer to Xilinx AR# 67885.

The recommended clock configuration is shown in the figure. MMCM(mod) is a modified version of the MMCM generated from the IP catalog and has the internal structure shown in the figure. In other words, clkPar, clkSerTx, and clkSerRX all originate from the same clock output, and clkPar is generated by dividing clkSer using BUFGCE_DIV. While this configuration minimizes skew between clocks, it introduces phase indeterminacy into clkPar due to the division process. Therefore, a clock signal phase-synchronized with the input modulation clock is generated separately (clk_clr), and this clock is used to perform a synchronous reset of the divider counter, thereby obtaining a clkPar that is phase-synchronized with the input. These modified MMCM and BUFG_CLR_DEV files are included in the support directory.

Because the modified MMCM are used, constraints that automatically assigned by IP (such as CLOCK_DELAY_GROUP via Matched Routing) do not apply. Manually add the following constraint to the project's XDC:

create_generated_clock -name clk_fast     [get_pins u_MMCM_CDCM/inst/mmcme4_adv_inst/CLKOUT0]
create_generated_clock -name clk_slow_CLR [get_pins u_MMCM_CDCM/inst/mmcme4_adv_inst/CLKOUT3]
create_generated_clock -name clk_slow     [get_pins u_MMCM_CDCM/inst/BUFGCE_DIV_CLK3_inst/O]

set_property CLOCK_DELAY_GROUP group_mmcm_cdcm_second [get_nets u_MMCM_CDCM/inst/clk_fast_TX]
set_property CLOCK_DELAY_GROUP group_mmcm_cdcm_second [get_nets u_MMCM_CDCM/inst/clk_fast_RX]
set_property CLOCK_DELAY_GROUP group_mmcm_cdcm_second [get_nets u_MMCM_CDCM/inst/clk_slow]
Figure 2: Clock configuration for the UltraScale FPGAs. Figure 3: Modified MMCM to provide the best clock skew adjustment.

docs.title: Method for Producing Modified MMCM
docs.text:
• Generate MMCM from IP catalog: Check the Optimize Clocking Structure box on the Clocking Options page, and set output clocks as shown in the figure. Set clk_slow_CLR to the same values as clk_slow (125 MHz, phase 0°). However, the actual phase of clk_slow is not determined until the CLR described below is applied. Set only clk_slow_CLR to BUFG; set the other three signals to Buffer. Check the Matched Routing box for all four signals. Additionally, since changing the order will alter the generated circuit, configure the four signals in the order shown in the figure.
Figure 4: Output Clocks configuration for MMCM.
  • Editing the Output Codes: Copy the two files generated by the IP (the wrapper file <IP name>.v and the main file <IP name>_clk_wiz.v), save them under different filenames, and use the edited code. Although CE and CLR are originally connected to fixed values, connect BUFDIV_CE and BUFDIV_CLR to them, respectively. Also, add the input ports for BUFDIV_CE and BUFDIV_CLR to both files.
Figure 5: How to edit the generated MMCM code.

docs.title: Dynamic Re-alignment of Clock and Data Phases
docs.text:
When using long optical fibers-typically around 1 km-it is necessary to address phase shifts between the clock and data caused by changes in ambient temperature. In the primary node of MIKUMARI link, the modulated clock signal returned from the secondary node is sampled using the primary node's own transmission clock. In this process, the phase between the clock and data is affected by changes in transmission delay caused by the fiber's expansion and contraction. In such use cases, the MIKUMARI link's upper-layer protocol must measure the phase between the clock and data, and if the variation exceeds a certain threshold, the IDELAY tap value must be readjusted. If the system is operated without readjustment, data sampling becomes unstable as the phase variation approaches the unit interval, eventually causing the link to go down. The temperature coefficient of SMF-28, a common optical fiber material, is 35 ps/km/K [1]. Based on this value and the environment in which you plan to use MIKUMARI link, please determine whether a readjustment mechanism is necessary.

[1] Slavík, R., et al., Sci Rep 5, 15447 (2015).

The current MIKUMARI link protocol provides the following signal ports for dynamic readjustment of the phase relationship:

  • reqIdelayShift: A signal received from the upper-layer protocol to shift the IDELAY tap value by ±1. Entering "01" or "10" allows the tap value to be dynamically increased or decreased. This input must be a one-shot relative to clkPar.
  • reqShutOffOut: This signal indicates that communication must be temporarily halted to perform a readjustment involving a change in bit positions when IDELAY is about to exceed its adjustable range. This request is a signal sent by the MIKUMARI link to the upper-layer protocol.
  • shutOffAckIn: An input signal indicating that the upper-layer protocol has received a request from the link and has temporarily halted data communication.

The figure below shows a flowchart of the procedures for ensuring stable communication during long-distance transmission using these signals. First, prepare some upper-layer protocol for measuring phase variations. For example, the use of a DDMTD-based ClockPhaseAnalyzer can be considered. The upper-layer protocol drives the reqIdelayShift signal as appropriate to adjust the tap values according to the phase variation. For example, when using IDELAYE2, this signal must be driven every 78 ps. At this time, it is strongly recommended to introduce hysteresis. When reqIdelayShift is received, the CBT adjusts the IDELAY settings immediately without halting the data communication.

Figure 6: Time series during phase readjustment

After issuing reqIdelayShift multiple times, if the phase deviation appears likely to exceed the range adjustable by IDELAY, the CBT issues reqShutOffOut. This signal indicates that the CBT wishes to realign the phase relationship, which involves changing bit positions. Since this process may corrupt data, communication must be temporarily halted to perform the realignment. When this signal becomes 1, the upper-layer protocol stops data communication at an appropriate time and then returns shutOffAckIn. This procedure must also be performed on the secondary node side. When the CBT completes the phase realignment, reqShutOffOut returns to 0. At that point, the upper-layer protocol resets shutOffAckIn to 0 and resumes communication.

This procedure is completed within 1 ms. The decision regarding when to halt communication after reqShutOffOut becomes 1 is left entirely to the upper-layer protocol. Since phase variations due to temperature changes are assumed to be gradual, there should be ample time to respond.
